title: Ginzburg's Night Battles: Microhistorical Recovery of Benandanti Folk Tradition
description: Carlo Ginzburg's I Benandanti (The Night Battles) was published in Italian in 1966 and appeared in English translation in 1983, transforming the methodology of witchcraft historiography. Working from Friulian Inquisition records, Ginzburg recovered the beliefs of the benandanti — a group of men and women who claimed to go out in spirit at night to fight witches in defense of crops — and traced how their self-understanding was gradually transformed through inquisitorial interrogation toward the standard sabbath-attending witch stereotype. The book demonstrated both that genuine folk beliefs independent of elite demonology existed, and that inquisitorial procedure systematically distorted such beliefs toward officially expected confessions. Ginzburg's microhistorical method — deep reading of a few sources for what cannot be spoken — became paradigmatic for the field.
historiographical_note: Ginzburg's Night Battles established the methodological and conceptual framework developed further in Ecstasies (1989). His argument that folk beliefs had a genuine pre-inquisitorial existence was contested by scholars like Cohn and Briggs who questioned whether the benandanti tradition could be recovered from behind the inquisitorial record. The tension between 'folk beliefs are real' (Ginzburg) and 'folk beliefs are inquisitorial projections' (Cohn) structures subsequent debate.
source_method: Ginzburg, I Benandanti (1966; English 1983); Friulian Inquisition records; subsequent scholarship
